newsitem.title: USA: Commerce nominee Daley defends department.
newsitem.headline: Commerce nominee Daley defends department.

text.p: Commerce Secretary nominee William Daley promised on Wednesday to keep politics out of his department and said it was essential to maintaining a strong U.S. economy.
Daley also said he would support sanctions against China if Beijing engaged in weapons proliferation activities.

"I want to make my position absolutely clear; there is no place for politics in the Department of Commerce," Daley said in written answers to questions submitted to him before his confirmation hearing before the Senate Commerce Committee. The questions and answers were released by the committee.
Daley, 48, was nominated by President Bill Clinton last month to succeed Mickey Kantor, who replaced Ron Brown after Brown was killed in a plane crash last April while on a trip to Bosnia.

Some former Commerce Department officials are being investigated for political campaign fundraising activity while at or after they left the department and critics have said too many posts at the department have been used for political appointees.
"The department's reputation has been sullied," Commerce Committee Chairman John McCain, R-Arizona, told Daley.

"If confirmed, there will be no connection between campaign contributions and making decisions on important departmental programmes, including participation in trade missions," Daley said in his written answers.

He said he would suspend all trade missions for 30 days while the procedures for deciding which business executives go on the trips were being reviewed. He also said he would cut the number of political positions at the department by 100.

Asked about the use of laws calling for trade sanctions against China if China engages in military proliferation activities, Daley replied, "I support implementing those laws and imposing sanctions if the facts of Chinese behaviour meet the test in the laws."
In his opening statement, Daley defended the department against congressional critics who say it serves little purpose and should be abolished.
"The Commerce Department is where America's potential and promise come together, where our future jobs are created and our economic growth is nurtured," Daley said.
He said the department was essential for promoting trade and providing reliable economic information.
Daley said he would insist on open and fair trade with U.S. trading partners. "We shouldn't leave our workers at risk from unfair trading partners," he said.

Daley, a Chicago lawyer, is the brother of Chicago Mayor Richard Daley. He said to avoid any perception of favouritism, he would not take part in any decisions at the department that involved Chicago as long as his brother serves as mayor.
